examples.text: Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web (WWW)!

To learn about a scientist and an invention, read a reliable biography, museum article, or science book. Record the scientist’s name, the invention, and the source. Compare sources when their accounts differ; a famous discovery is not always an invention.

Where can I find information about a scientist for my report?

You can gather information from secondary sources like books, biographies, encyclopedias, and articles in newspapers or on websites.
Eyeglasses help people who see blurry so they can see the world clearly.

Ask an adult at home about an invention they use, such as a radio. Record its name, what it does, and how it changes a daily task. Separate what the person reports from your own guess. Compare the account with a reliable book or museum source.

How did the radio change the news?

Radio changed the news! News, storm warnings, and music reached millions of homes at the same time, even without internet or TV.

Fuel is anything that can burn, like wood, paper, or gasoline!
Iron turns into flaky rust when it reacts with both oxygen and water!
Decomposers like bacteria, fungi, and worms do the rotting! They break apart biodegradable waste and return its nutrients to the soil.
Burning dried cogon grass in the fields is a chemical change that produces smoke and ash.
Burning is a chemical change! Wood turns into ash and gases, and you can never turn it back into wood again.
When paper burns, it turns into ash and smoke. It can never become paper again!

Why should you never burn plastic trash?

Burning plastic releases toxic chemical gases into the air, so you should never burn trash in an open fire!

Why shouldn't we burn our trash?

Burning trash, especially plastic, releases poisonous smoke bad for our health! It's better to sort, recycle, or compost it instead.
Never mix liquid bleach with ammonia-based cleaners! It creates a toxic chloramine gas, which is very dangerous.
Using proper toilets keeps human waste from mixing into the water we drink.
Compost returns nutrients to the soil so plants can grow stronger and healthier.
Compost is dark, rich, soil-like material made from rotted plant and food scraps.

With your teacher, survey a school waste problem using the same questions for each participant. Group and classify the responses, then communicate the findings to your class. Stay open-minded: listen to different opinions and change your explanation when evidence supports a better one.
Survey questionnaires can help gather information about environmental issues and concerns in a school or community.

When a muscle pulls, the bone it's attached to moves like a lever turning at the joint.
Some of your bones act like hard armor, protecting the soft organs tucked safely inside your body.
Your digestive system is a team: mouth, esophagus, stomach, small intestine, and large intestine all work together to break down food and absorb nutrients.
The circulatory system transports oxygen, nutrients, and hormones to all parts of the body and removes waste products like carbon dioxide.
Your respiratory system — nose, trachea, and lungs — works together to bring oxygen into your blood and remove carbon dioxide!
A plant's roots soak up water and nutrients from the soil so the whole plant can use them.
After the root grows, a shoot pushes upward out of the soil, reaching toward the sunlight!
The shoot system includes the stem, leaves, and other above-ground structures that help the plant grow and survive.
The tamaraw lives in the grasslands, forests, and mountains of Mindoro.
Carp is another kind of freshwater fish that farmers raise in fishponds.
Bats fly in the air at night! This makes them aerial animals, even though they are mammals.

How can you easily see different habitats?

A diagram showing a carabao on land and a bangus in water makes their different habitats easy to see!
The gumamela, or hibiscus, is a big, colorful flower commonly planted in Philippine gardens!

Make a habitat table with plants and animals from the Philippines. Examples: garden—gumamela and butterflies; rice field—rice and frogs; seashore—beach grasses and crabs; mangrove swamp—mangrove trees and fish. Record what you actually observe; not every habitat contains every example.
The tikling is often seen walking through rice fields, grasslands, and wet areas.

Mangroves grow in salty water along the coast, right where the sea meets the land!

Both butterflies and moths go through four life stages: egg, caterpillar, pupa, and adult.

Draw and compare these stage sequences: butterfly—egg, caterpillar, pupa, adult; frog—egg, tadpole, froglet, adult; chicken—egg, chick, adult; human—developing baby in the womb, baby, child, adolescent, adult. Reproduction connects adults to a new generation. A chicken or human has no pupa stage.
A frog's life has four stages: eggs laid in water, a tadpole with a tail and gills, a froglet with four legs and a tail, then an adult frog with four legs and no tail.

Draw and compare these stage sequences: butterfly—egg, caterpillar, pupa, adult; frog—egg, tadpole, froglet, adult; chicken—egg, chick, adult; human—developing baby in the womb, baby, child, adolescent, adult. Reproduction connects adults to a new generation. A chicken or human has no pupa stage.
A baby chicken, called a chick, hatches out of an egg.

Cattle are herbivores, so they eat grass and leafy plants.
A goat is a herbivore -- it eats grass, leaves, and small plants.
Crocodiles are carnivores — they eat meat like fish, birds, and other animals.
Pigs are omnivores, so they eat both plants and meat.
The civet, or alamid, is an omnivore that eats fruit, insects, small animals, and eggs.

Draw this Philippine food chain: rice plant → grasshopper → frog → snake. The arrows point from the food to the eater, showing energy transfer. Label the grasshopper a herbivore and the frog and snake carnivores. This is one possible chain, not every feeding relationship.

Why does the food chain arrow point that way?

In a food chain, the arrow always points to the eater — because that's the direction energy flows, from food to the one eating it.

Draw this Philippine food chain: rice plant → grasshopper → frog → snake. The arrows point from the food to the eater, showing energy transfer. Label the grasshopper a herbivore and the frog and snake carnivores. This is one possible chain, not every feeding relationship.
People are part of food chains too — as omnivores we eat plants like rice and vegetables and animals like fish and chicken, connecting us to the Sun through our food.

Rigid objects are hard and cannot be easily bent, deformed, or compressed, like a stone or a chair.
Before testing, sort your objects into rigid and soft groups! Then, guess which group will change shape more easily.
Soft objects can be easily bent, deformed, or compressed, like a sponge, bread, or cloth.
Before testing, sort your objects into rigid and soft groups! Then, guess which group will change shape more easily.
Before testing, sort your objects into rigid and soft groups! Then, guess which group will change shape more easily.
A great record for a shape-change test is a table! It needs columns for the object, shape before, force used, and shape after.

What units do we use to measure distance?

We measure distance in units such as meters and kilometers!

With your teacher, mark a straight start and finish line. Measure the distance between them with a meterstick or tape measure. Start a stopwatch when the toy car crosses the start line and stop it at the finish. Record distance in meters and elapsed time in seconds. Repeat using the same marks. Compare trials; your reaction time can change the stopwatch reading.
We measure time in units such as seconds, minutes, and hours! Tick-tock!

With your teacher, mark a straight start and finish line. Measure the distance between them with a meterstick or tape measure. Start a stopwatch when the toy car crosses the start line and stop it at the finish. Record distance in meters and elapsed time in seconds. Repeat using the same marks. Compare trials; your reaction time can change the stopwatch reading.
Average speed is the total distance divided by the total time for the whole trip!
If two things travel the exact same distance, the one that takes less time is the faster one!
On a distance-time graph, the slope shows your average speed! A steeper line means you're going faster, while a flat line means you've stopped moving.
On a distance-time graph, a steeper line means faster movement, while a flat line means standing still. You can easily tell the speed just by looking at the line's shape!

Draw a distance–time graph with time in seconds horizontally and distance in meters vertically. Plot (0, 0), (1, 2), (2, 4), and (3, 6). Joining these points gives a straight rising line: 2 meters each second is constant speed. Label both axes and units.

On the same distance–time graph, label the horizontal axis Time (s) and the vertical axis Distance travelled (m). At times 0, 1, 2, 3 s, plot A: 0, 0, 0, 0 m; B: 0, 1, 2, 3 m; C: 0, 2, 4, 6 m. Join each set with a line. A is stationary; B and C have uniform speeds. C is faster because it travels farther each second. Compare slopes only on the same axis scales.

Which axis shows time and which shows distance?

The x-axis is the horizontal line at the bottom and usually shows time. The y-axis is the vertical line going up and usually shows distance.

A force can speed up, slow down, or completely change the direction of a moving object!

With your teacher, roll a soft ball slowly on a clear, level surface. Predict and test: a gentle push along its motion can speed it up; a gentle opposing push can slow or stop it; a sideways push can turn it. Record the motion before and after each push. Keep each trial separate. A push need not make a moving object immediately travel in the direction of the push.

A force is needed to change an object's motion—to start it, stop it, or change its direction!
You need a force to start a still object moving, and another force to stop it!

Pulling the ends of a rubber band apart applies a stretching force that makes the band longer and thinner.
A stretched rubber band stores elastic potential energy. When released within its elastic limit, it returns toward its original shape. This ability to recover its shape is called elasticity.
Bending a piece of clay or a soft wire changes its shape by curving it without cutting or breaking it.

With your teacher, predict and record each change. Push soft clay with a flat palm; it flattens. Pull a strip of dough at both ends; it stretches. Bend another strip into a curve. Twist a soft cloth by turning its ends in opposite directions. Squeeze a sponge between your palms. Compare each shape before and after. A push or pull can change shape as well as position.
Solid materials can be changed by cutting, tearing, folding, twisting, bending, stretching, and pressing.

When you put two like poles together, they push apart and repel each other!

What happens when you test different objects with a magnet?

Things made of iron are attracted! But plastic, rubber, and wood will not be pulled.
Some objects have both magnetic and non-magnetic parts! A magnet sticks to the steel blades of scissors, but not the plastic handles. It depends on the part you test!
Test it yourself! Touch paper clips to a magnet. The most clips stick at the ends or poles, proving the poles are the strongest parts!

What happens when you test different objects with a magnet?

Things made of iron are attracted! But plastic, rubber, and wood will not be pulled.
A magnet is amazing because it can pull iron even without directly touching it!
The Sun warms your skin through radiation! It sends invisible infrared waves right through the empty vacuum of space to reach you.
Very loud sounds can damage the tiny parts inside your ear and weaken your hearing.
Energy is simply your ability to do work or cause a cool change to happen!
Light is a form of energy, and plants use it to make their own food!
Sound is a form of energy that travels as a wave, moving outward from a vibrating source.
We see objects because light hits them and bounces right back into our eyes!
Bamboo can be turned into musical instruments like the flute, because air vibrates inside its hollow stem to make sound.
In a dapog stove, burning firewood releases heat that cooks delicious food!
Sandy soil drains water super fast after rain! But clay soil holds moisture and turns into sticky mud.

Sand has larger mineral particles than silt, and clay has the smallest of these three. Loam combines sand, silt, and clay. These different particle mixtures help explain why soils hold and drain water differently. Compare samples rather than judging only by color.

Loam has both big and small pores! This means it drains well, yet still stores water for plants.

With your teacher, put equal volumes of dry sandy, clay-rich, silty, and loamy soil in identical filter-lined funnels. Pour the same measured volume of water into each. Collect and measure the water that drains out after the same time. Repeat. Compare the results; soil texture and packing affect drainage. Water retained is not all available to roots.

Animals need food, water, air, and shelter to live. Plants need water, air, sunlight, and nutrients from the soil.

Why do more wild greens grow in the rainy season?

Rain gives plants the water they need to grow, so more wild greens grow — and grow faster — making saluyot and talinum easier to find!
Animals need food, water, air, and shelter to live. Plants need water, air, sunlight, and nutrients from the soil.
River water is fresh, meaning it is not salty like the sea! Because of this, many animals and plants depend on rivers for clean water.

With your teacher, grow the same kind and number of seeds in different soils. Keep pot size, soil volume, planting depth, light, and watering schedule the same. Use several pots for each soil. Measure plant heights on the same days and compare records. Report your observations even if they disagree with your prediction.

What should you write before planting a soil test?

Before planting, write a hypothesis that predicts which soil type will grow the tallest plant!
For a soil experiment, plant the exact same number of seeds at the same depth in each pot of different soil!

Temperature is the degree of hotness or coldness of the air around us, and it changes with the time of day and the weather.
A barometer measures air pressure, and it helps us forecast the weather!

How do we measure how fast the wind is blowing?

We measure wind speed using a spinning instrument called an anemometer!
A wind vane shows which direction the wind is coming from! It spins so its pointer always faces into the wind.
Humidity is the amount of water vapor in the air, and we measure it using a hygrometer!
Catch the rain! A rain gauge is the instrument that measures the rainfall.

How do scientists measure how cloudy the sky is?

Cloud cover is measured in oktas — eighths of the sky! When it's 8/8 oktas, the whole sky is covered by clouds.
A thermometer measures temperature — it tells you how hot or cold the air, water, or your body is!
A barometer measures air pressure, and it helps us forecast the weather!

How do we measure how fast the wind is blowing?

We measure wind speed using a spinning instrument called an anemometer!
A wind vane spins to show where the wind comes from! If it blows from the north, we call it a north wind.
Humidity is the amount of water vapor in the air, and we measure it using a hygrometer!
Catch the rain! A rain gauge is the instrument that measures the rainfall.
Place your rain gauge in an open area away from trees and buildings. They can block the rain and make the reading wrong!
Philippine schools can set up a simple weather station! With a thermometer, rain gauge, and wind vane, students learn by recording their own weather data.

With your teacher, record weather readings with times and units from the same instruments and places. Example: at 8 a.m., 26 °C and partly cloudy; at noon, 30 °C and cloudy. The air became 4 °C warmer and cloud cover increased. This does not prove rain will fall. Check current local forecasts and warnings before planning outdoor activities.
A weather chart tracks if it's sunny, rainy, or cloudy every day, helping us spot patterns in the weather!

If you hear thunder, go with an adult immediately to a substantial building or an enclosed hard-top vehicle. Crouching outdoors does not make you safe. Stay away from isolated trees and open shelters. Wait inside until at least 30 minutes after the last thunder.

What is the Sun mostly made of?

The Sun is mostly made of hydrogen, along with some helium!

How does the Sun's size compare to Earth?

The Sun is about 109 times wider than the Earth. It's truly massive!
Solar energy comes directly from the bright light and cozy heat of our sun!
The upright, pointed part of a sundial that casts a shadow is called the gnomon! It blocks sunlight to form a shadow that points to the time.

With your teacher, keep a shadow stick fixed in one place. At different times, mark its shadow’s tip and record the length and direction. Earth’s rotation makes the Sun appear to change position, so the shadow changes too. Observe the shadow, never look directly at the Sun.

With your teacher, keep a shadow stick fixed in one place. At different times, mark its shadow’s tip and record the length and direction. Earth’s rotation makes the Sun appear to change position, so the shadow changes too. Observe the shadow, never look directly at the Sun.
In the morning, the shadow points west because the sun is in the east; a shadow always points away from the light.

With your teacher, keep a shadow stick fixed in one place. At different times, mark its shadow’s tip and record the length and direction. Earth’s rotation makes the Sun appear to change position, so the shadow changes too. Observe the shadow, never look directly at the Sun.

How does a sundial tell time?

It’s an old clock that uses a stick's shadow in sunlight! The shadow moves as the Earth rotates to show the time of day.

With your teacher, keep a shadow stick fixed in one place. At different times, mark its shadow’s tip and record the length and direction. Earth’s rotation makes the Sun appear to change position, so the shadow changes too. Observe the shadow, never look directly at the Sun.
The sun is the original source of energy for almost every food chain on Earth!

How do we know our Sun guesses are right?

After class, check a trustworthy book or science site! This confirms our ideas about sunshine instead of just voting on them.

Where can we check facts about sunlight and weather?

A PAGASA or NASA education page is a trustworthy secondary source! You can use it to confirm class ideas about sunlight and weather.
